title: Bihar-Born Kanishka Narayan Becomes UK's First Minister for Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: The 36-year-old Labour MP, who moved from Muzaffarpur to Cardiff at age 12, has been elevated to a newly created cabinet-level AI role under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Kanishka Narayan is the UK's first Minister for Artificial Intelligence, appointed under PM Andy Burnham.
  • The new role emphasizes AI as a cabinet-level priority, spanning multiple government departments.
  • Narayan previously served as Parliamentary Under-Secretary for AI and Online Safety since September 2025.
  • He became Wales' first ethnic minority MP in the 2024 general election, with degrees from Oxford and Stanford.
  • His appointment reflects a growing trend of Indian-origin politicians in senior government roles.
Kanishka Narayan's Journey
November 1989
Born in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, India.
2001
Moved to Cardiff, Wales at age 12.
2024
Elected as Wales' first ethnic minority MP.
July 2025
Appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary for AI and Online Safety.
July 20, 2026
Appointed UK's first Minister for Artificial Intelligence.
  • Kanishka Narayan, born in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, has been appointed the UK's first-ever Minister for Artificial Intelligence under new PM Andy Burnham.
  • The newly created role sits across the Department for Business and Trade and the Cabinet Office, elevating AI policy to cabinet-level priority.
  • Narayan previously served as Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for AI and Online Safety under Keir Starmer since September 2025.
  • He became Wales' first ethnic minority MP in the 2024 general election and holds degrees from Oxford and Stanford.

A New Role for a New Era

Kanishka Narayan, the Indian-origin Labour MP for Vale of Glamorgan, was appointed the United Kingdom's first Minister for Artificial Intelligence on July 20, according to an official government announcement. The newly created position, established under incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham, marks a significant upgrade from Narayan's previous junior ministerial role and signals the UK government's intent to treat AI as a standalone cabinet-level policy priority.

https://x.com/10DowningStreet/status/2079350751965376774

The role sits across the Department for Business and Trade and the Cabinet Office, giving Narayan a cross-departmental mandate to shape AI regulation, investment strategy, and industrial policy. He had served as Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for AI and Online Safety since September 2025 under then-PM Keir Starmer, overseeing the AI Security Institute, semiconductor strategy, and the government's Tech for Growth initiative.

"The stability of the depth of our relationship with India is a stability we'll continue to see in the months and years ahead."

— Kanishka Narayan, Minister for Artificial Intelligence
> **"His appointment comes amid a record number of Indian-origin MPs in the UK Parliament."**

"His appointment comes amid a record number of Indian-origin MPs in the UK Parliament."

From Bihar to Westminster

Narayan's path to the cabinet is a story of improbable mobility. Born in November 1989 in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, he moved to Cardiff with his family at age 12. The family shared a one-bedroom flat off City Road, where Narayan slept on the floor. He spent a year at Cathays High School before winning a scholarship to Eton College.

From Eton, he went to Balliol College, Oxford, to study Philosophy, Politics and Economics, then earned an MBA from Stanford University. Before entering politics, Narayan worked as a civil servant in the Cabinet Office under David Cameron and at the Environment Department, later moving into private-sector financial advisory work.

He joined the Labour Party at 18 and was elected to Parliament in July 2024, becoming Wales' first ethnic minority MP — a milestone the BBC compared to Lady Megan Lloyd George becoming Wales' first woman MP in 1929.

AI Policy Elevation
›New role established under PM Andy Burnham.
›Cross-departmental mandate across Business and Trade and Cabinet Office.
›Focus on AI regulation, investment strategy, and industrial policy.
›Plans to purchase £400 million in AI chips.

AI Policy and the India Connection

As AI minister, Narayan has been an active voice on frontier AI regulation. In a wide-ranging interview at Cambridge's India Day earlier this year, he described the UK's approach as "robust on outcomes, pragmatic on means." Under his watch, the UK forced social media platform Grok to pull back a nudification feature and built what he described as the world's only AI lab with pre-deployment access to frontier models.

Narayan has also been a vocal champion of UK-India tech ties. He attended the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February 2026 and visited his birthplace in Bihar for the first time in over two decades, meeting JD(U) leader Sanjay Kumar Jha to discuss AI collaboration between the UK and the state.

At the inaugural India All Party Parliamentary Group celebration in Parliament, Narayan pointed to the ratified UK-India Free Trade Agreement as evidence of deepening bilateral ties. "The Labour Party has been a deep friend of India for a significant period of time, right from the very outset as a big champion in support of Indian independence," he said.

Representation Matters
›1.9 million people of Indian heritage in the UK.
›Growing number of Indian-origin MPs in UK Parliament.
›Narayan's ties to India enhance representation in AI policy.

What This Means for the Diaspora

Narayan's elevation is the latest in a growing pattern of Indian-origin politicians reaching senior government positions across Western democracies. His appointment comes amid a record number of Indian-origin MPs in the UK Parliament. For the estimated 1.9 million people of Indian heritage living in the UK, having someone with deep personal ties to India at the center of the country's AI strategy adds a layer of representation in one of the most consequential policy areas of the decade.

What's Next

Narayan's immediate priorities in the expanded role will likely include the UK's semiconductor investment strategy — the government recently announced plans to purchase £400 million in AI chips — and navigating the regulatory balance between fostering AI innovation and managing safety risks. His cross-departmental mandate under Burnham suggests AI policy will be more tightly integrated with trade and industrial strategy than under the previous structure.
